newsitem.title: TAIWAN: China to hold manoeuvres near rival Taiwan - report.
newsitem.headline: China to hold manoeuvres near rival Taiwan - report.

text.p: China plans military drills on its coast across from rival Taiwan this month to warn the island against inciting "disturbances" with its own exercise before Hong Kong's return to China, a newspaper reported on Tuesday.

Taiwan, which has set a major annual exercise for June 23-24, said it had detected no troop mobilisation on the southeastern Fujian coast, where Hong Kong's independent Sing Tao Daily said the mainland exercises would be staged.
"As of now, we have not noticed signs of communist troops planning to hold large-scale exercises," Taiwan defence ministry spokesman Kong Fan-ting told reporters.
"Please be assured that we will closely monitor any movements by communist troops," Kong added.

The Sing Tao report quoted unidentified sources as saying Beijing feared that Taipei -- its arch rival since a civil war split them in 1949 -- would try to arouse military tension in the Taiwan strait to mar Hong Kong's July 1 return to China's rule and planned the manoeuvres as a warning.
"The purpose is to prevent any disturbance during the Hong Kong handover," the newspaper said.
Taiwan has said its late-June exercise was unrelated to the Hong Kong handover despite the sensitive timing.
Taiwan's exercise was expected to showcase a range of new high-technology weapons, including F-16 and Mirage 2000-5 fighters recently imported from the United States and France.
Also slated for testing are several radar-evading Lafayette-class "stealth" frigates bought from France and U.S.-made Patriot anti-missile defence systems, Taiwan media have said.
Beijing considers Nationalist-ruled Taiwan a renegade province that must be brought under the mainland's eventual rule -- by force if it makes moves toward independence.
Beijing held eight months of war games, amphibious landing practices and unarmed ballistic missile tests near Taiwan in the run-up to the island's March 1996 presidential election.

China vows to attack Taiwan if the island tries to declare independence and assailed the election -- the first popular poll for a Chinese leader -- as a cloaked attempt by Taipei to pursue separatism.
The exiled Republic of China on Taiwan officially espouses reunification with the mainland, but not before Beijing's ruling Communist Party embraces pluralism and gives up its monopoly on power.
